text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--A new survey shows that 208 major Danish firms lost a total of 162 million crowns in 1996 through fraud carried out by staff, typically falsifying bills and putting private purchases through company accounts. The figures correspond to 29 percent of Danish firms being cheated in this way, compared to an average 52 percent in the rest of Europe.

--Denmark's two biggest trade unions, SiD (general workers) and Metal, have both expressed their opposition to government proposals to set up funds financed by firms to employ disabled and handicapped workers.

--Denmark's environmental ministry still refuses to allow canned drinks onto the Danish domestic market, defying threats by the European Commission to take the matter to the European court. In a new report the ministry repeats its refusal on environmental grounds to permit aluminium tins or drop Denmark's current bottle deposit system.

--Copenhagen Business High School professor Michael Moeller says that it is unrealistic for Danes to think that they get free, impartial financial advice from their banks. Banks are commercial companies and their clerks are salesman, so if consumers believe they are getting the best advice free of charge from their banks they are naive, a bank consultant whose services you do not pay for is a salesman, he said.

--Danish finance minister Mogens Lykketoft says the government will focus on reducing the record 270,000 early retired Danes by introducing special job schemes for the elderly in a campaign to be launched this autumn.

--A Labour victory in Britain's upcoming general elections, might endanger the planned merger of Bass and Carlsberg-Tetley, meaning potential major earnings losses for the Danish brewer in the U.K. market and explaining Goldman Sachs latest downgrading of Carlsberg.
